# input: # No number agreement of any kind: Chinese marks plurality nowhere on a noun,
# so every unit here has exactly one printed form and 1 and 5 take the same
# word. The separators are English's — "," for groups, "." for the decimal.
# No space between the number and the unit, on input or output. `Printer`'s
# `gap` is empty for this language, which is what makes the round trip hold:
# the engine reads back its own "2,000克" byte for byte.
# 公斤 and 公吨 are the everyday words and 千克 and 吨 are the printed ones —
# two spellings per unit, and only one of each pair on the way out.
# The myriad. Chinese counts in ten-thousands, so 万 is a magnitude word in its
# own right and 一万 is one of them, not ten of a thousand.
# A spelled cardinal has to reach the kilogram through 公斤, because 千克 opens
# with 千 — the numeral reader takes the "thousand" and leaves 克 behind, and
# "二百零五千克" does not parse at all.
# The word operators need whitespace around them even though Chinese is
# written without any: 乘 and 除以 are matched as separate tokens, and
# "2千克乘3" does not parse. The symbol operators above have no such
